full_judgment:
AK Badrul Huq J: It is wretchedness to record message that many litigants in order to steer clear of order /judgment/decree maintained by last ladder of hierarchy adopt dubious role and take recourse to ingenious methods including filing of fraudulent litigation to rout order/judgment and decree of Court. Seekers of justice in whose favour verdict had been passed are to wait and wait to receive fruit of verdict and justice and they become victims of justice in hands of unscrupulous litigants.

2. The present matter in hand is an apt illustration how judgment and decree awarded in favour of decree-holder here defendant-petitioner by Court of appeal which have been maintained by Appellate Division rendering final touch has been ventured to be thwarted by judgment-debtors and persons litigating under judgment-debtors.

3. Refusal to reject plaint of first-fifth-opposite parties on point of bar of law as embodied in Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure (for short the Code) prompted defendant-petitioner to approach this Court in Civil revision petition under section 115 of the Code.

4. Portrayal of essential facts forming background of this revision petition as emerged from Revision Petition, annexures annexed in Petition, judgments of Courts awarded in earlier proceeding and papers produced before this Court will be instructive in resolving war of words and these are succinctly put down hereunder:

A. Petitioner of civil revision petition Sreemati Purabi Rani Barmani as plaintiff on 3-1-1984 laid a suit being Title Suit No. 5 of 1984 in Fourth Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Dhaka for a decree of Partition in respect of Nine annas and Thirteen gondas share which came to 10.25 acres from total divisible 17.13 acres of property. Petitioner, also, sought other incidental and consequential reliefs in suit. Suit was, thereafter, renumbered as Title Suit No. 88 of 1985 and, again renumbered as, Title Suit No. 81 of 1992 in Fourth Court of Assistant Judge, Gazipur.

B. Hasen Ali was defendant No. 4 in Title Suit No. 5 of 1984. Summons had been duly served upon him. On his death his heir sons Insad Ali. Emdadul Huq, Dhukai Mia, Ead Ali, Naib Ali, Sohrab Hossain, Idris Ali. Bellaluddin, Alauddin, wives Billatunnessa and Rasatunnessa and daughters Rasheda Khatoon, Surja Banoo. Kanchan Bala, Laljan Bibi and Jobeda Khatoon had been substituted as defendant Nos. 4(ka)-4(Tha). Summons and registered notices upon substituted Defendant Nos. 4(ka)-4(Tha) had been issued and duly served upon them. defendant Nos. 1-3 Arfan Ali, Akbar Ali contested the suit in laying written statement.

C. Title Suit No. 81 of 1992 did not meet with success. Suit stood dismissed. Judgment and decree is dated 31-12-1996. Appeal being Title Appeal No. 22 of 1997 carried by petitioner as appellant was crowned with success. Appeal was allowed. Judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 81 of 1992 was set aside. Suit was decreed in preliminary form. In the appeal defendant Nos. 4(Ka-Tha) had been respondents.

D. Learned Assistant Judge, though, dismissed the suit found that some land in the name of Bhabuk Barman was recorded as vested property and defendant admitted the suit land to be under possession of plaintiff.

E. Learned Appellate Judge in awarding decree in favour of petitioner positively found:

i. Plaintiff-(petitioner) is daughter of Durgacharan.

ii. Bhabuk had 0.59 acres of property and that 0.59 acres of property had been claimed as vested property and Government failed to prove that the property was of Bhabuk and it was treated as vested property.

iii. Plaintiff (petitioner) as heir daughter of Durgacharan is the owner of entire 10.25 acres of property. Judgment and decree of the appellate Court is dated 30-7-1998.

F. Defendant Nos. 1 and 2 Erfan Ali and Akbar Ali having felt aggrieved of above adjudication approached the High Court Division in a revision petition under section 115 of the Code. Revision petition had been numbered as Civil Revision No. 4651 of 1998. Rule obtained stood discharged by a Single Bench of High Court Division. Judgment is dated 25-7-2001. High Court Division concurred with the finding reached by Court of appeal that Durgacharan succeeded 10.25 acres of property and after his death plaintiff (petitioner) inherited the said property. Finding of Court of appeal below was based upon proper appreciation of evidence on record. Judgment was followed by a decree drawn up on 14-8-2001.

G. Unsuccessful termination of Civil Revision case before the High Court Division could not deter defendants to make a halt. They went to Appellate Division in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1562 of 2001. Appellate Division by judgment dated 20-5-2002 dismissed Leave Petition. In recording dismissal Appellate Division held that learned Counsel for petitioner (Defendant) could not improve the case of the defendant to show that plaintiff (petitioner) was not the daughter of Durgacharan and Mr Bhuiyan failed to assail finding of fact arrived by lower appellate Court and then of High Court Division which discharged Rule on merit by hearing parties.

H. Final decree of Partition had been drawn up on 21-11-2002.

I. Substituted defendant Nos. 4(cha) and 4(jaha) Sohrab Hossain and Alauddin as plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2 (first and second-opposite parties) and Md Quayyum Molla, Mohammadullah and Golam Kibria as plaintiffs (third-fifth opposite parties) filed a suit being Title Suit No. 76 of 2001 in Second Court of Joint District Judge, Gazipur. Reliefs sought are:

(1) A decree declaring ownership of plaintiffs in respect of 7.35 acres of land described in schedule 'A' to the plaint be passed in favour of plaintiffs and against defendants.

(2) A decree declaring that the decree passed in Title Suit No. 86 of 1995 of the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Fourth Court, Gazipur on the basis of judgment and decree dated 30-7-1998 passed in Title Appeal No. 22 of 1997 in respect of 'A' schedule land is fraudulent, collusive, malafide, inoperative, null and void, illegal and not at all binding upon the plaintiffs.

(3) Other incidental reliefs had been, also, sought.

J. First-fifth-opposite parties by way of petition for amendment of plaint under Order VI, rule 17 of the Code sought insertion of the number of Title Suit as "81 of 1992" in place of "86 of 1995". The petition was allowed by Court and Title Suit No. "81 of 1992" stood substituted in place of "86 of 1995".

K. Case projected in plaint is that Durgacharan Barman died leaving behind two daughters namely, Sukhi Barmani and Bishika Rani Barmani alias Bishaka Barmani. Sukhi Barmani died unmarried and Bishika Rani Barmani became absolute owner and possessor of 10.25 acres of property left by Durgacharan Barman. Bishika Barmani died leaving behind only son Bhabuk Chandra Barman who became exclusive owner of 10.25 acres of property by way of inheritance. Bhabuk Chandra Barman by a registered deed of exchange dated 23-9-1999 transferred 4.00 acres of property in favour of plaintiff No. 1. Bhabuk Chandra Barman, thereafter, by registered deed dated 1-4-2001 sold 1.05 acres of property to plaintiff Nos. 2-4. Bhabuk Chandra again sold 1.00 acres of property in favour of plaintiff No. 5 by a registered sale deed dated 1-4-2001. Further case is that plaintiff No. 1 by way of Heba became owner of 0.22 acres of property and plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2 became owners in respect of 0.08 acres of property by way of inheritance. The plaintiffs, thus, become owners in possession over 7.35 acres of property.

L. In the suit decree-holder-petitioner Purabi Rani Barmani was made defendant No. 3.

M. Petitioner on presentation of a petition under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code sought rejection of plaint canvassing basic grounds which are:

1. In Title Suit No. 5 of 1984 which was renumbered as Title Suit No. 81 of 1992, Hasen Ali, father of plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2 (present first and second opposite parties) was defendant No. 4 and on his death plaintiffs Nos. 1 and 2 (first and second opposite parties) and other heirs of Hasen Ali were substituted and summons upon them had been duly served and in spite of due service of summons they did not appear in the suit. End Ali, the son of Hasen Ali, stood in the witness box as defendant's witness.

2. Property of Bhabuk was recorded in SA khatian No. 148 and his address having been shown in India, Deputy Custodian of Vested Property was made defendant No. 5 and defendant No. 5 contested suit on presentation of a written statement.

3. Preliminary decree had been passed on 30-7-1998 in Title Suit No. 81 of 1992 and the deeds dated 23-9-1999 and 1-4-2001 were created by plaintiff Nos. 1-5 (first-fifth opposite parties) after preliminary decree and on the basis of above deeds plaintiffs (opposite parties) got no right to file the suit and suit is barred under the principles of res judicator.

4. Suit land of Title Suit No. 81 of 1992 and suit land of present Title Suit No. 76 of 2000 are same and inseparable.

5. Bhabuk, transferor of deeds of plaintiffs (opposite parties) was represented by Deputy Custodian of vested Property.

6. Over the same subject matter in between the parties and their representatives further litigation is barred by law.

N. Learned Joint District Judge, Second Court, Gazipur by order dated 7-8-2002 rejected the petition laid under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code. Reasons which weighed with learned Joint District Judge in recording rejection are:

i. Preliminary decree passed in Title Suit No. 81 of 1992 was not disposed of finally.

ii. Suit was not only for partition but, also, for declaration and parties are not same and the suit did not appear to be barred by principles of resjudicata.

5. Feeling aggrieved, petitioner approached this Court in this Revision Petition.

6. First-fifth-opposite parties put up resistance to revision petition on laying affidavit-in-opposition controvert statements made in revision petition. Basic contentions tabled in affidavit-in-opposition is that suit is not hit by principles of res judicata under section 11 of the Code.

7. Contentions pressed into service from side of petitioner are catalogued hereunder:

i. Controversy in respect of heir ship of petitioner Sreemati Purabi Rani Barmani as daughter of Durga-charan and her right, title, interest and possession for an area of 10.25 acres which was the suit property in Title Suit No. 81 of 1992 was finally adjudicated and determined by highest Court of land and same matter cannot be reopened and reagitated by opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 and other opposite party Nos. 3-5 who claimed title from Bhabuk Barman and the suit is barred by law and plaint is liable to be rejected under inherent power of Court under section 115 of the Code if not under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code.

ii. Seeking declaration that decree passed in Title Suit No. 81 of 1992 of the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Gazipur on the basis of judgment and decree dated 30-7-1998 passed in Title Appeal No. 22 of 1997 in respect of schedule land is fraudulent, collusive, malafide, inoperative, null, void and not binding upon plaintiffs is absolutely barred by law and plaint is liable to be rejected in exercise of inherent power under section 115 if not under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code.

Guiness Peat (Trading) Limited vs Md Fazlur Rahman, 44 DLR (AD) 242. Abdul Jalil and others vs Islamic Bank Bangladesh Ltd and others, 53 DLR (AD) 12 and T Arivandandam vs TV Satyapal and another, AIR 1977 SC 2421 have been relied upon in support of contentions pressed.

8. Contentions raised from side of petitioner have been given rejoinder in bringing home contention from side of first-opposite parties which are:

i. Plaint cannot be rejected on question of resjudicata and question of resjudicata can be decided only on production of evidences at the time of trial.

ii. Decree passed by appellate Court which was maintained by High Court Division and Appellate Division against opposite parties is an ex parte decree and not a contested decree and an ex parte decree even if maintained by Appellate Division can be very much challenged in a suit and plaint, thus, cannot be rejected as barred by law.

Sreemati Pushpa Rani Das and another vs AKM Habibur Rahman and others, 1993 BLD (AD) 217 had been pressed in aid of contention raised.

9. In the wake of contentions advanced from both parties, the kernel question that survives for determination is whether plaint can be rejected either on the strength of provision envisaged in Order VII, rule 11 or in inherent power of Court embodied in section 151 of the Code.

10. In approaching the question principles of law on res judicata embodied in section 11, Order VII, rule 11 and inherent power envisaged in section 151 of the Code can be explored.

11. Doctrine of res judicata has received a statutory sanction in the Code as a matter of prudence and to give due weightage to a finding or decision so as to reach finality in the matter of a dispute between the same parties or litigating under the same parties. The doctrine, thus, is to achieve finality of dispute between parties being a principle of prudence so as to give efficacy to a finding of Court rather than permit the parties to go to trial more or less on the same issues over again. Judicial verdict has its special sanctity and cannot be the subject matter of discussion at any future time involving identical or similar issues. The doctrine of res judicata or constructive res judicata predominantly is a principle of equity, good conscience and justice. In Cari-Zeiss Stiftung vs Rayner and Keeler Ltd and others (1967). The Law Reports: Appeal Cases 853 = (1966) 2 All ER it has been aptly stated by Lord Upjohn that the broader principle of res judicata is founded on twin principles so frequently expressed in Latin that there should be an end to litigation and justice demands that the same party shall not be harassed twice for the same cause.

12. Order VII, rule 11 of the Code deals with power of Court to reject a plaint. Rule contemplates that stillborn suit should be nipped in the bud at its inception so that no further time is consumed on a fruitless litigation. A suit which is on the face of it incompetent under law should not be allowed to further encumber legal proceedings. If the suit is barred by law it is the statutory duty of Court to reject plaint.

13. Section 151 of the Code does not formulate any new doctrine but only a Legislative recognition of well-known doctrine and principle that every Court has inherent power to act ex debitio justitiae to do that real justice for administration of which alone it exists. Under section 151 Court acts ex debitio justitiae according to equity, justice and good conscience of a case and in consonance with fundamental principles of judicial procedure. It has been ruled by Superior Courts of sub-continent that a plaint may be rejected under the provision of Order VII, rule 11 and if plaint cannot be rejected under Order VII, rule 11 same can be very well rejected in exercise of inherent power under section 151.

14. Law on the subject has been spelt out, discussed and considered in good number of cases of our jurisdiction as well as foreign jurisdiction. Of those Burma!! Eastern Ltd vs Burmah Eastern Employees Union and others, 18 DLR 709 may profitably be taken notice of. High Court considered the rejection of plaint matter under the provision of Order VII, rule 11 and in considering it laid down the principle that a plaint can be thrown in limini if not under Order VII, rule 11 then under Court's inherent power. Murshed CJ speaking for the Court observed at Paragraph No. 10:

Order 7, rule 11 of the Code as quoted above, enumerates certain categories under which the Court is called upon to reject a plaint, but, it is obvious that they are not exhaustive. It appears from the language of rule 11 of Order 7 that it requires that an incompetent suit should be laid at rest at the earliest moment so that no further time is wasted over what is bound to collapse as not being permitted by law.

It has been, also laid down in Paragraph No. 11:

A suit may be specifically barred by law and, in such an event, the matter would come under the express terms of clause (d) of rule 11 of Order VII of the Code. But, even in a case where a suit is not permitted by necessary implication of law in the sense that a positive prohibition can be spelt out of legal provisions, the Court has an inherent jurisdiction to reject the plaint. This really amounts to saying that Order 7, rule 11, is not exhaustive. Hardly any authority is needed for such a proposition. I may, however, refer to some decisions on this point.

Murshed CJ in the case, also considered other authorities notably, amongst others, are Thakur Haribar Bakhsh Singh vs Thakur Jagannath Singh, AIR 1924 Oudh 413 and Radhakishen vs Wali Md AIR 1956 Hyderabad 133.

15. In the yardstick of the above stated principles and enunciation of law by Superior Courts the question posed now shall be answered.

16. In Title Suit No. 5 of 984 then renumbered as Title Suit No. 81 of 1992 petitioner was plaintiff. Predecessor of first and second-opposite parties Hasen Ali had been defendant No. 4 and on his death his heirs sons, daughters and wives including first and second-opposite parties had been substituted and first and second opposite parties were substituted as defendant Nos. 4(cha) and 4(Jaha), From certified copy of service return which has been produced before this Court it stood exposed to view that summons upon substituted defendants including substituted defendant Nos. 4(cha) and 4(Jaha) (first and second opposite parties) had been duly served and there was a declaration made by serving officer as to the service of summons upon them. From certified copy of order dated 7-2-1996 it is brought to light that learned Assistant Judge made a note in the order sheet that summons upon substituted defendants had been duly served. Learned Judge further noted that registered notices were kept with the record. Service of summons upon substituted defendants including substituted defendant No. 4(cha) and 4(jaha) who are (first and second opposite parties) is an evidence as to the service of summons as contemplated in rule 19A of Order V of the Code. The noting as to the due service of summons upon substituted defendants including defendant Nos. 4 (cha) and 9(jaha) (first and second opposite parties) dated 7-2-1996, also, got a strong presumption as mandated in section 114(e) of The Evidence Act of 1872.

Out of 17.13 acres of property opposite parties claimed property is 7.35 acres of land. Schedule property in both the suits are exactly the same.

19. In Title Suit No. 81 of 1992 petitioner as plaintiff set up her claim over 10.25 acres of property as the daughter of Durgacharan. In Title Suit No. 76 of 2001. First-fifth opposite parties put up claim in respect 7.35 acres of property out of petitioner's decreed 10.25 acres of property of Title Suit No. 81 of 1992 raising contention that petitioner is not daughter of Durgacharan and Bhabuk Chandra Barman inherited 10.25 acres of property as daughter's son of Durgacharan and Bhabuk being owner and possessor of 10.25 acres of property transferred 4.00 acres of property by way of registered deed of exchange dated 23-9-1999 in favour of first-opposite party and then Bhabuk by way of registered deed dated 1-4-2001 sold 1.05 acres of property to second-fourth-opposite parties and, thereafter, Bhabuk transferred 1.00 acre of property by a registered sale deed dated 1-4-2001 in favour of fifth-opposite party. First and second opposite parties by way of Heba and inheritance claimed 1.22 acres of property from their father Hasen who was defendant No. 4 in Title Suit No. 82 of 1992.

20. Learned Senior Assistant Judge as Trial Judge in Title Suit No. 81 of 1992 in his Judgment positively found that some property in plot No. 205 had been recorded in the name of Bhabuk as vested property and lease taken by defendant No. 1 in respect of 0.59 acres of property was absolutely illegal. Learned Trial Judge dismissed suit not on the point that petitioner is not the daughter of Durgacharan but on the point that she got no possession on such property.

21. Learned Subordinate Judge, First Court, Gazipur as Appellate Judge taking into consideration evidences and materials on record positively rendered decision that Durgacharan having been dead his property was inherited by his two daughters Bishika Rani Barmani and Purabi Rani Barmani alias Prabhati Barmani and Bishaka Rani Barmani having been dead without any son Purabi Rani Barmani inherited the entire 10.25 acres of property left by Durgacharan and Purabi Rani Barmani became the owner and possessor of entire 10.25 acres of property. Appellate Judge, also, categorically found that Government who was defendant No. 5 in suit failed to prove that Bhabuk had been owner of 0.59 acres of property out of suit property that is 10.25 acres of property and Bhabuk left for India and said 0.59 acres of property had been vested property. The Appellate Judge rendered decision that government failed to prove that Bhabuk had been owner of 0.59 acres of property. Learned Appellate Judge in allowing the appeal granted a preliminary decree to the extent of nine annas and thirteen gondas which came to 10.25 acres of property. Finding reached by Appellate Judge that Durgacharan inherited 10.25 acres of property and on the death of Durgacharan petitioner inherited said property rested on proper appreciation of evidence and the finding had been maintained by High Court Division and as well as by Appellate Division.

22. Case projected by first-fifth-opposite parties in plaint is that Durgacharan died leaving behind two daughters namely, Sukhi Barmani and Bishika Rani Rarmani alias Bishaka Barmani and Sukhi Rani Barmani died unmarried that Bishika Rani Barmani alias Bishaka Barmani became absolute owner and possessor of 10.25 acres of property left by Durgacharan and Bhabuk Barman got entire 10.25 acres of property. In view of firm decision recorded by Appellate Judge as to inheritance, ownership and possession in respect of entire 10.25 acres of property of Durgacharan by petitioner Purabi Rani Barmani and, also, as to non-ownership of Bhabuk over 0.59 acres of property which had been maintained by Appellate Division the claim put forward by first-fifth-opposite parties that Bhabuk Barman inherited 10.25 acres of property from her mother Bishika Rani Barmani and that first-fifth opposite parties by way of exchange and sale deeds from Bhabuk Barman and, also, of Heba and inheritance from predecessor Hasen. defendant No. 4 of earlier suit acquired ownership and title over 7.35 acres of property out of petitioner's decreed 10.25 acres of property stand absolutely barred by law and first-fifth-opposite parties cannot be allowed to reopen the matter which reached to its finality by highest Court of land that is the Appellate Division.

23. Preliminary decree had been passed on 30-7-1998 by appellate Court which, also became a decree of Trial Court. Appellate judgment is dated 30-7-1998. Judgment passed by High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 4651 of 1998 is dated 25-7-2001. Judgment of Appellate Division is on 20-5-2002. Final decree had been drawn up on 21-11-2002. Deed of exchange and other deeds of first-fifth-opposite parties are dated 23-9-1999 and 1,4,2001 which are after a long period of preliminary decree and during pendency of Civil Revision case before High Court Division.

24. This drives us to a legal aspect of the matter of a great public importance which is relief sought by opposite parties. Relief sought in respect of decree passed by Appellate Court has been stated earlier.

25. Decree passed by Court of appeal stood merged in decree of High Court Division and that decree was maintained by Appellate Division. Can a decree which stood merged in decree of High Court Division and sustained by Appellate Division be challenged in a Court Subordinate to High Court Division and, also, Appellate Division? Answer is in firm negative. If suit in hand is allowed to be proceeded with and not buried at doorstep majesty of law and administration of justice shall break down and sanctity of judgment and decree of Superior Court shall be flung to the wind and dubious and unscrupulous litigants shall be encouraged to lay misconceived and fraudulent cases to challenge Judgments passed by the Apex Court. This tendency of dishonest litigants deserves to be taken serious note of and curbed by recording appropriate order and issuing necessary direction including imposing of exemplary costs in the interest of the majesty of law and administration of justice.

26. Coming now to contention advanced from side of first-fifth-opposite parties that decree passed was ex-prate and not contested against opposite parties and decree. though, maintained by Appellate Division can very much be challenged before Subordinate Court.

27. This contention does not hold water at all and can be ruled out without any hesitation. Decree is decree whether contested or ex parte and all decrees contested or ex parte got purity and carry force of law. Ex parte decree cannot be impaired on ground of its being ex parte. It has earlier been posited that summons upon first and second opposite parties who were substituted defendant Nos. 4 (cha) and 4(jaha) had been duly served and learned Judge made a note as to due service of summons upon all substituted defendants. First and second opposite parties allowed the suit to be directed ex parte against them.

28. The authorities relied upon from side of petitioner and first-fifth-opposite parties now may be taken heed of.

29. Authorities relied upon from side of petitioner shall be addressed now. In Guiness Peat (Trading) Limited vs Md Fazlur Rahman (Supra), plaintiff-respondent instituted a Money Suit before Third Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka asserting that defendant, a Trading company of London, offered to plaintiff by telexes to sell 150 metric tons of skimmed milk of Hungarian origin as per specification. On arrival at Chittagong Port plaintiff rejected the goods, but for mitigating loss sold away the same. In the plaint it had been averred that cause of action of suit arose on 12th March, 1982 when Letter of Credit was opened in favour of defendant. Appellate filed an application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code for rejection of the plaint on the ground that Court had no jurisdiction since the defendant did not reside or carry on business within jurisdiction of this Court. Bar of suit contemplated under rule 11(d) was not pleaded and bar of cause of action postulated in rule 11(a) was pressed into service.

Appellate Division held:

"In considering an application for rejection of a plaint the specific provision under Order VII, rule 11 should ordinarily be followed. A resort to section 151 of the Code may be made in the interest of justice only in an exceptional case where the suit is foredoomed and if it is allowed to be proceeded with it will amount to an abuse of the process of the Court."

30. In Abdul Jalil and others vs Islamic Bank Bangladesh Ltd and others (Supra). petitioner as plaintiff earlier instituted a suit in Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka for declaration of title and partition of suit properties. The suit on contest was dismissed by trial Court which decree was affirmed up to the Appellate Division. Petitioner then instituted a suit in Fifth Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka praying for declaration that decree passed in earlier Title Suit was illegal and invalid and was not applicable in respect of 'Ga' schedule land of present suit. Before trial Court defendants filed an application under Order VII, rule 11 read with Order 14 rule 2 of the Code for rejection of plaint of Title Suit No. 92 of 1991. Learned Subordinate Judge as Trial judge rejected defendant's prayer for rejection of plaint. Against which defendants moved before High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 2757 of 1999 and a Division Bench by judgment dated 18th November, 1999 made the Rule absolute and rejected plaint under Order VII, rule II of the Code. Plaintiffs took a Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal before Appellate Division. Appellate Division laid down:

It is settled that where a plaint cannot be rejected under Order 7 rule 11 of the Code the Court may invoke its inherent jurisdiction and reject the plaint taking recourse to section 151 of the Code.

Appellate Division further held:

"The present suit cannot be allowed to be proceeded further. As the ultimate result of the suit is as clear as daylight such a suit should be properly buried at its inception so that no further time is consumed in a fruitless litigation. When the ultimate result is clear, the plaintiffs cannot be allowed to re-open the same matter afresh after losing up to the Appellate Division. This is merely a gambling in litigation which cannot be allowed."

31. In T Arivandandam vs TV Satyapal and another, (Supra) a sorry story of a long drawn out series of legal proceedings, revealing how father of the petitioner contested an eviction proceeding, lost it, appealed against it, lost it again, moved a Revision only to be rebuffed by summary rejection by High Court and, thereafter, Court's generosity in the matter of granting time to vacate the premises had been fully exploited by the father of the petitioner and the suit of the petitioner set upon a clever adventure in filing a suit before Fourth Additional First Munsif, Bangalore for a declaration that the order of eviction which had been confirmed right up to High Court was one obtained by "fraud" and collusive had been portrayed. Observation of eminent Judge VR Krishna lyer who spoke for Court is couched in the following terms:

The trial Court would insist imperatively on examining the party at the first hearing so that bogus litigation can be shot down at the earliest stage. The Penal Code is also resourceful enough to meet such men, and must be triggered against them. The trial Court in this case will remind itself of section 35A, CPC and take deterrent action if it is satisfied that the litigation was inspired by vexatious motives and altogether groundless.

Further observation framed in the following language:

The pathology of litigative addiction ruins the poor of this country and the Bar has a role to cure this deleterious tendency of parties to launch frivolous and vexatious cases.

The long arm of the law must throttle such limitative caricatures if the confidence and credibility of the community in the Judicature is to survive. The contempt power of the Court is meant for such persons as the present petitioner.

32. This brings us to the authority placed from the side of opposite parties. Before adverting to the authority it is always to be borne in mind that a decision is only an authority for what it actually decides, it cannot be quoted for a proposition that may seem to follow from it. Every judgment must be read applicable to the particular facts proved or assumed to be proved since the generality of expression which may be found therein are not intended to be exposition of whole law but governed or qualified by the particular facts of the case in which such expression occurs. What is of the essence in its decision is its ratio and not every observation found nor what logically followed from the very observation made in it. It is not a profitable task to extract a sentence or word from a judgment divorced from the context of the question under consideration.

33. In Sreemati Pushpa Rani Das and another vs AKM Habibur Rahman and others (Supra), defendants filed an application for rejection of plaint on ground that previously between parties, a suit being Title Suit No. 78 of 1977 was filed by respondent and the same was withdrawn and the cause of action of that suit is same and defendant brought Title Appeal No. 93 of 1990 in the same Court for permanent injunction and got decree on contest and against which respondent filed Title Appeal No. 100 of 1991 and, as such, present suit was not maintainable as barred by res judicata. The Appellate Division held that whether the suit was barred by res judicata or not was a matter to be decided at the time of trial and the same cannot be decided from a reading of plaint. The fact and circumstances of the case relied upon got no bearing in fact and circumstances of case in our hand. In cited case Title Suit No. 78 of 1979 was withdrawn and right and title of parties had not been finally adjudicated and Title Suit No. 93 of 1990 for permanent injunction was dismissed and Title Appeal had been filed. No finality had been attached by any decision by Superior Court but in case in hand judgment and decree reached to finality by highest Court of land i.e. Appellate Division.

<u>34. The judicial verdict awarded by Appellate Court which is final Court of fact as to inheritance of petitioner Purabi Rani Barmani from her father Durgacharan in respect of entire 10.25 acres of property and former's ownership and possession over that 10.25 acres of property and, also, as to Bhabuk Barman's non-ownership over 0.59 acres of property out of said 10.25 acres which was maintained by last ladder of hierarchy, that is Appellate Division cannot be allowed to be challenged in a suit laid by first-fifth-opposite parties. Plaint is to be nipped in the bud and it merits rejection. In equality, good conscience and administration of justice and, also, in interest of majesty of law and sanctity and finality of verdicts of superior Court inherent power under section 151 of the Code requires to be invoked and exercised to bury suit of first-fifth-opposite parties at the threshold if not under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code.</u>

35. Before parting we are inclined to record an observation that no litigant has a right to lay fraudulent, shady, ill-motivated and untenable proceeding in a Court of law when those cases are throttling the functioning of justice dispensation system which itself is groaning under unbearable arrears and backlogs. For blameworthy conduct of these types of unprincipled and dishonest litigants compensatory cost is to be awarded upon them.

36. Corollary thereof is, that Rule arising out of civil revision petition under section 115 of the Code got merit and it succeeds. Rule is made absolute. Order dated 7-8-2002 passed by learned Joint District Judge, Second Court, Gazipur in Title Suit No. 76 of 2001 refusing to reject plaint stands set aside. Plaint of Title Suit No. 76 of 2001 of said Court stands rejected.

Regard being had to the blameworthy conduct of first-fifth-opposite parties we award a compensatory cost of Taka 5,000 upon first-fifth-opposite parties. Cost shall be paid to petitioner who is being dragged to further malafide and fraudulent litigation.

End.
